title: Management of Receivables
outcomes: Explain the costs and benefits of receivables.
Evaluate credit standards, terms and policy changes.

meta.exam_tip: Use a columnar statement for each policy; compare net benefit, not just sales.

concepts.title: Objectives and costs of receivables
body: Receivables arise from credit sales; they boost sales and customer relationships but tie up funds and carry risk.
Costs of receivables: capital cost (funds locked), administrative cost (credit checks, collection), collection cost, and default cost (bad debts). Benefits: higher sales and contribution.
The objective is to optimise investment in receivables so that the incremental benefit of extra sales exceeds the incremental costs.
concepts.analogy: Credit is a sales tool with a price tag.
concepts.work: Extending credit to a new dealer network can add sales but also overdue risk.

concepts.title: Credit policy: standards, terms and evaluation
body: Credit standards decide which customers get credit, using the 5 Cs — character, capacity, capital, collateral and conditions — and sources like bank references, credit rating agencies and trade references.

Credit terms: credit period, cash discount (e.g. "2/10, net 30") and collection policy. Longer credit and laxer standards raise sales and receivables and bad debts; discounts speed collections at a cost.

Evaluation (incremental or total approach): compare contribution gained with added cost of funds on receivables (valued at cost or at sales), bad debts, discounts and collection costs. Adopt the policy with the highest net benefit.
concepts.analogy: Change credit only if the extra contribution beats the extra costs.
concepts.work: Offering 2% for payment in 10 days may shrink receivables enough to pay for itself.

concepts.title: Monitoring receivables and factoring
body: Monitoring: days sales outstanding (receivables ÷ average daily credit sales), ageing schedules (buckets like 0–30, 31–60, 61–90, over 90 days), and collection matrix.

Factoring: a factor buys receivables and manages collection; with recourse (firm bears bad debts) or without recourse (factor bears them). Benefits: quicker cash, reduced collection effort; costs: commission and interest on advances. Forfaiting applies to export receivables, typically medium-term and without recourse.
Other tools: securitisation, bill discounting, credit insurance and electronic platforms like TReDS for MSME receivables.
concepts.analogy: Watch the age of receivables, not just the total.
concepts.work: A rise in the "over 90 days" bucket is an early warning of bad debts.

illustrations.title: Loosening credit terms
illustrations.q: Current credit sales ₹50 lakh with 30 days' credit and bad debts 1%. Extending credit to 60 days is expected to raise sales to ₹60 lakh with bad debts of 2%. Variable cost is 60% of sales; required return 15%; use 360 days and value receivables at variable cost. Should the firm extend credit?

solution.text: Proposed policy adds ₹2.77 lakh — extend credit.

illustrations.title: Should we factor?
illustrations.q: Annual credit sales ₹120 lakh. A without-recourse factor charges 2% commission and takes over collection. This saves bad debts of 1% of sales and administration cost of ₹1.5 lakh. Ignoring finance charges, is factoring worthwhile?

solution.text: Factoring is marginally beneficial; any advance at an interest cost below the firm's cost of funds would add further benefit.

checks.label: Net benefit of factoring before finance effects (₹ lakh)

jobs.title: Collections review
jobs.situation: DSO has risen from 45 to 70 days.
steps: Identify customers responsible for overdue amounts.
Consider discounts or factoring for slow payers.
jobs.takeaway: A few large overdue accounts usually explain a rising DSO.

mcqs.q: Which is NOT one of the 5 Cs of credit?
mcqs.explain: The 5 Cs are character, capacity, capital, collateral and conditions. In practice: use credit reports.
mcqs.topic: Credit policy: standards, terms and evaluation

options: 2% discount if paid in 10 days; otherwise full amount in 30 days
mcqs.explain: The discount rewards early payment within 10 days; the net amount is due in 30. In practice: cost of forgoing is high.
mcqs.topic: Credit policy: standards, terms and evaluation

mcqs.q: Annual credit sales ₹36 lakh; receivables ₹6 lakh; 360 days. DSO:
mcqs.explain: 6 ÷ (36 ÷ 360) = 6 ÷ 0.1 = 60 days. In practice: compare with credit terms.

mcqs.q: In factoring without recourse, bad debts are borne by:
mcqs.explain: Without recourse the factor takes the credit risk, charging more. In practice: with recourse the seller bears it.
More generous terms attract sales but lengthen collection. In practice: evaluate incremental costs.
mcqs.topic: Credit policy: standards, terms and evaluation

options: Receivables classified by how long they have been outstanding
mcqs.explain: It highlights overdue amounts. In practice: prepare monthly.

mcqs.q: Cost of funds on receivables (₹40 lakh sales, 45 days, variable cost 75%, return 12%, 360 days):
mcqs.explain: Receivables at cost = 40 × 0.75 × 45/360 = ₹3.75 lakh × 12% = ₹45,000. In practice: state the valuation basis.
mcqs.topic: Credit policy: standards, terms and evaluation

mcqs.explain: Forfaiting buys export receivables, usually without recourse. In practice: often backed by bank guarantees.

summary: Costs: capital, admin, collection, bad debts.
traps: Contribution, not sales, is the benefit of extra credit.

viva.q: What are the costs of holding receivables?
viva.model: Capital cost of funds tied up, administration and collection costs, and losses from bad debts.

viva.q: How is a change in credit policy evaluated?
viva.model: By comparing the incremental contribution with incremental costs of funds on receivables, bad debts, discounts and collection.
Days sales outstanding: receivables divided by average daily credit sales, showing how long customers take to pay.

viva.q: Distinguish factoring with and without recourse.
viva.model: With recourse the seller bears bad debts; without recourse the factor bears them.
An electronic platform where invoices of MSME suppliers on large buyers are discounted by financiers.

cases.title: Delta Textiles
cases.case: Delta Textiles has credit sales of ₹72 lakh a year (360 days) and receivables of ₹18 lakh. It considers offering "2/10, net 45"; 50% of customers would take the discount, cutting DSO to 25 days.

mcqs.explain: 18 ÷ (72 ÷ 360) = 18 ÷ 0.2 = 90 days. In practice: far above terms.

mcqs.q: New receivables at 25 days DSO (₹ lakh):

mcqs.explain: 50% × 72 × 2% = 0.72. In practice: compare with interest saved.
mcqs.topic: Credit policy: standards, terms and evaluation

mcqs.q: At a 12% cost of funds, interest saved on ₹13 lakh released (₹ lakh):
mcqs.explain: 13 × 12% = 1.56 > 0.72 discount cost — the discount pays. In practice: also check bad debt effects.
mcqs.topic: Credit policy: standards, terms and evaluation
